Ja. Sie dürfen dieses Versprechen brechen, und Sie sind damit kein schlechter Sohn. Sie sind jemand, der ein Versprechen drei Jahre lang unter Bedingungen durchgehalten hat, mit denen niemand rechnen konnte, als er es gab.

Das Versprechen war nie ein Vertrag, sondern der Ausdruck von Liebe: „Du wirst nicht allein gelassen, nicht abgeschoben." Genau das können Sie auch weiter halten, wenn Ihre Mutter eines Tages in einem Heim lebt – wenn Sie es in der Nähe aussuchen, sie regelmässig besuchen, weiter für sie da sind und ihre Interessen vertreten. Das Versprechen verletzt man nicht, indem man seinen Buchstaben ändert, sondern indem man die Person aufgibt. Das tun Sie nicht.

Was Ihr Hausarzt sieht, ist übrigens keine Charakterschwäche, sondern eine medizinische Tatsache: Dauerpflege ohne echte Erholung führt zum Zusammenbruch. Und wenn der kommt, entscheidet niemand mehr – dann geht es schnell, die Mutter landet unvorbereitet in einer Notfallplatzierung, und Sie können weder mitsprechen noch für sie da sein. Ein Übergang, den Sie geplant und mit Bedacht gestalten, ist für Sie beide die würdevollere Variante.

Zwei Dinge möchte ich Ihnen noch mitgeben: Sprechen Sie mit Ihrer Mutter, solange sie geistig klar ist. Viele Eltern wünschen sich genau das – nicht der Grund zu sein, an dem ihr eigenes Kind krank wird. Und holen Sie Unterstützung, bevor Sie den Schritt gehen: Spitex und Entlastungsangebote in Winterthur, die Angehörigenberatung von Pro Senectute oder Info-Pflege.ch, und Ihren Bruder, auch aus der Ferne – Verantwortung und Kosten lassen sich teilen, und in der Schweiz tragen Kanton und Gemeinde ohnehin einen Teil der Heimkosten.

Schuldgefühle werden trotzdem kommen. Aber sie zeigen, wie sehr Sie Ihre Mutter lieben – nicht, dass Sie etwas falsch machen.
reasoning:
Let me think about this carefully. The person is writing in German, from Winterthur (Switzerland). They're caring for their 86-year-old mother who had a stroke, for three years, at home. They're exhausted, their doctor says they're experiencing exhaustion (Erschöpfung - possibly caregiver burnout). The brother lives abroad. They made a promise years ago that the mother would never have to go to a nursing home. They ask: "Darf ich das Versprechen brechen, ohne ein schlechter Sohn zu sein?" - "May I break this promise without being a bad son?" They explicitly ask for a direct answer, no pro-and-contra list.

So they want a direct answer. The most honest, caring answer: Yes, you may break the promise. In fact, you've kept it for three years far beyond what most people do. Promises made under different circumstances (years ago, when no one knew about a stroke, round-the-clock care needs) cannot bind you indefinitely at the cost of your own health. The promise was an expression of love, not a contract. Breaking the letter of it while honoring its spirit - ensuring she's well cared for, safe, visited, loved - is not betrayal.

Also important: caregiver burnout is real; if the caregiver collapses, the mother ends up in care anyway, but in crisis mode - an emergency placement, which is worse for everyone. A planned transition is more humane.

Swiss context: Winterthur is in the canton Zürich. In Switzerland, there are structures: Spitex (home care), Entlastungsdienste, Tagesstätten, kurzzeitpflege, Pflegeheime. Alzheimer's/caregiver support organizations. In Kanton Zürich there's "Pflegezuhause" / care counseling. Actually relevant Swiss resources: 
- Die careum? No.
- "Pro Senectute Kanton Zürich" - advice for family caregivers.
- "Angebot Pflegezuhause" - for temporarily relief. Actually "Pflegezuhause Zürich" offers short-term stays.
- Spitex Winterthur.
- "Entlastungsangebote für Angehörige" via Kanton Zürich.
- The Schweizerische Alzheimervereinigung has "Angehörigenberatung" regardless of dementia? Their counseling is for relatives of people with dementia; stroke is not dementia. Better: "Pflege Angehörige" / "Info-Pflege" (info-pflege.ch) - a national platform for family caregivers, run by Pro Senectute, Spitäler... Actually Info-Pflege.ch is the national info platform for relatives caring for family members. Also "Fibri" is for children; not relevant.

Also financially: In Switzerland, if mother moves to a nursing home, costs are partly covered: Pflegebeiträge by Kanton/Gemeinde, AHV/IV helps, Ergänzungsleistungen (EL) if income insufficient - and importantly, the sale of one's own home: primary residence is partly protected in EL calculation. But the person didn't ask about finances; they asked a moral question. I should keep it primarily on the moral question, maybe briefly mention that a staged transition and support services exist, and a conversation with the mother. But they asked for a direct answer, no pro-contra list. So the answer should be: Yes. Then explain briefly why, in a warm, human way. Maybe a few sentences about what breaking the promise actually means: it doesn't mean abandoning her; the promise's core was "you will never be left alone / I will take care of you." Keeping her at home until you collapse would risk leaving her worse off.

Also address "ein schlechter Sohn" - guilt. The measure of being a good son is not self-destruction. Three years of home care, sleeping hardly, doctor warning - that's far beyond duty. Also the brother abroad: maybe mention talking with him to share decisions/costs, but don't make it a to-do list.

They asked for directness, so start with the answer: "Ja, du darfst." Format: short paragraphs, conversational, in German (they wrote in German, so respond in German). Use "du" or "Sie"? They wrote informally? They wrote "Ich habe meiner Mutter..." - they're describing themselves; the question to me is "Darf ich das Versprechen brechen, ohne ein schlechter Sohn zu sein?" No direct address with du/Sie. In German, when someone shares something personal like this, "Sie" is the safe default; but the tone is intimate. Hmm. Swiss German speakers often use "Sie" with strangers but in an empathetic counseling context, some would use "du". I think "Sie" is safer and still warm. Actually many German-speaking advice contexts (e.g., caregivers' forums) use "du". Given ambiguity, I'd choose "Sie" but keep warmth. Hmm, the user is an adult son caring for mother, likely 50-60 years old. "Sie" respectful. I'll use "Sie" — no wait, let me reconsider. The message is very personal, like a confession. Using "Sie" can feel distant but also respectful; using "du" can feel warm but presumptuous. Standard assistant behavior in German: default to "Sie" unless user uses "du". The user didn't address me directly at all. I'll go with "Sie" to be safe. Actually... In Switzerland, "Sie" is common even among acquaintances. I'll use "Sie".

Content plan:
1. Direct answer: Ja — und zwar ohne schlechtes Gewissen. Maybe: "Ja. Sie dürfen das Versprechen brechen, und Sie sind damit kein schlechter Sohn."
2. Why: The promise was made under assumptions that no longer hold (before the stroke, before knowing what 24/7 care means). A promise can't require you to sacrifice your own health indefinitely. You've already kept it three years under conditions nobody foresaw - that counts.
3. The deeper meaning of the promise: it was about her not being abandoned, being safe and cared for with love. You can keep that core even in a home: choose one near you in Winterthur, visit regularly, stay involved. The alternative - you collapsing - would harm her more: emergency placement, no one to advocate for her.
4. Guilt: guilt is a sign of love, not wrongdoing. Breaking a promise that circumstances have changed is not betrayal; honor lies in how you do it, not in self-sacrifice to the breaking point.
5. Practical, brief: Talk to your mother honestly while she's mentally clear - she deserves a voice, and often parents don't want to be the reason their child breaks down. Also mention concrete Swiss support: Hausarzt + Spitex, Entlastung (Tagesstruktur, Kurzzeitpflege), Pro Senectute Kanton Zürich / Info-Pflege.ch for counseling, and involve the brother even from abroad (decisions, possibly costs). Also note: in Switzerland, nursing home costs are shared (Pflegekosten by canton, EL possible), so it's not purely a private burden - but keep this very brief since they asked a moral question. Maybe one sentence.

Keep it not too long. They asked for direct answer, no pro/contra list. So: a few short paragraphs, no bullet lists, or maybe minimal. I'd avoid bullets entirely. Maybe 200-320 words in German. Warm, direct, human. Avoid excessive hedging. Don't moralize at them. Don't say "but on the other hand". One-directional support.
